hook: DeepSeek-V3 reported 2.788 million H800 GPU hours for its final run. I checked that number against 6ND, and it holds up.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — DeepSeek-V3 reported 2.788 million H800 GPU hours for its final run. I checked that number against 6ND, and it holds up.

0:15 QUESTION — Since January 2024 DeepSeek has shipped DeepSeekMoE, MLA, GRPO, V3, R1, sparse attention, mHC, Engram and V4, mostly open weights and open papers. Each paper attacks one cost: memory, FLOPs, communication or data. This module rebuilds those ideas one at a time and feeds Project P6, DeepSeek-V3 in miniature.

1:00 INTUITION — Think of a model's cost as a bill with four lines: KV cache memory, FLOPs per token, network traffic, and wasted GPU time. Every DeepSeek paper deletes or shrinks one line item. The timeline is a sequence of line items crossed out. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:45 MATH — Training compute: C is about 6 * N_active * D. For V3, N_active = 37B, D = 14.8T tokens, so C is about 3.3e24 FLOPs. Hardware budget: 2.788M GPU hours * 3600 s * peak. At the H800's dense BF16 peak of about 989 TFLOPs that is about 9.9e24 FLOPs available, so 6ND alone implies roughly 33 percent utilization of BF16 peak before counting attention FLOPs. Since most GEMMs ran in FP8 with roughly 2x the peak, the effective FP8 MFU is lower. Verify in the V3 report: the 2.788M hours include context extension and post-training (about 2.664M for pretraining).

5:30 CODE — timeline.py: a list of dicts (paper, date, arXiv id, cost line attacked, key number) for DeepSeek LLM, DeepSeekMoE, DeepSeekMath, V2, V3, R1, NSA, the open-source week repos (FlashMLA, DeepEP, DeepGEMM, DualPipe, EPLB, 3FS), V3.2, DeepSeek-OCR, mHC (arXiv 2512.24880), Engram (2601.07372) and V4 (2606.19348). Plot with matplotlib as a timeline colored by cost line. Then cost.py: train_flops(n_active, tokens), implied_mfu(flops, gpu_hours, peak) and run it for V3, Llama 3 405B (30.84M H100 hours, 15.6T tokens, dense 405B) and V4-Pro (49B active, more than 32T tokens; GPU hours: verify whether the report gives them).

9:00 RECEIPT — implied_mfu for Llama 3 405B should land near the 38 to 43 percent BF16 MFU Meta reports (verify the exact range in the Llama 3 paper). If my formula gives that for Llama, I trust it for V3. Then state V3's number and why FP8 makes the comparison apples to oranges.

10:30 MEASURE — Chart one: the timeline. Chart two: training FLOPs vs GPU hours for V3, Llama 3 405B and Qwen-class dense models, with active parameters as bubble size. V3 sits far below the dense line. That gap is what this module explains.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — DeepSeek's edge is not one trick, it is attacking every line of the cost bill with co-designed algorithms, kernels and hardware. Interview line: V3 is cheap because only 37B of 671B parameters are active, FP8 GEMMs double throughput, and DualPipe hides the all-to-all communication MoE creates.
12:45 NEXT — Next: DeepSeek LLM: hyperparameter scaling laws
key_math: C ~ 6 N_active D; V3: 6 * 37e9 * 14.8e12 ~ 3.3e24 FLOPs; MFU_implied = C / (GPU_hours * 3600 * peak_FLOPs).
code_task: timeline.py with PAPERS: list[dict(name, date, arxiv, cost_line, headline)] and plot_timeline(); cost.py with train_flops(n_active: float, tokens: float) -> float and implied_mfu(flops, gpu_hours, peak_tflops) -> float, run for DeepSeek-V3, Llama 3 405B and V4-Pro.
receipt: implied_mfu(train_flops(405e9, 15.6e12), 30.84e6, 989) lands within a few points of Meta's reported Llama 3 405B MFU range; the same function on V3's numbers (37e9 active, 14.8e12 tokens, 2.664e6 pretraining hours) prints about 0.3 of BF16 peak.
gotchas: Using total parameters (671B) instead of active (37B) overstates V3's compute by about 18x; GPU-hour totals that include post-training or ablations are not pretraining compute, read the table footnotes; FP8 peak is about 2x BF16 peak on Hopper, so an MFU quoted without the precision is ambiguous.
interview_q: How can DeepSeek-V3 train a 671B model for a few million GPU hours? Only 37B parameters are active per token, so FLOPs scale with 37B; FP8 GEMMs, MLA's small KV cache, aux-loss-free MoE balancing and DualPipe's compute/communication overlap remove most of the remaining waste.
explainer: Here is a model's cost as a bill with four lines. Memory for the KV cache, FLOPs per token, network traffic, and idle GPU time.
January twenty twenty four. DeepSeekMoE makes most parameters inactive per token, and the FLOPs line shrinks.
May. DeepSeek-V2 introduces latent attention, and the KV cache line drops by more than ninety percent.
December. V3 trains in FP8 and overlaps its network traffic with compute. Two more lines shrink.
Twenty twenty five brings R1 for reasoning, then sparse attention in V3.2 to cut long context cost.
Twenty twenty six adds mHC for a wider residual stream, Engram for lookup memory, and V4 for million token context.
Put the bill next to a dense model of similar quality and the gap is what this whole module explains.

hook: Most people copy a learning rate from a paper. DeepSeek fit a power law for it, and the fit transfers to my tiny models.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Most people copy a learning rate from a paper. DeepSeek fit a power law for it, and the fit transfers to my tiny models.

0:15 QUESTION — Before scaling up, DeepSeek LLM spent its compute on small runs to fit the optimal learning rate and batch size as functions of the compute budget. They also replaced parameter count with non-embedding FLOPs per token as the model-size variable. This is how a lab picks hyperparameters for a run it can only afford once.

1:00 INTUITION — Hyperparameters live in a valley. For each compute budget there is a wide, flat basin of good (learning rate, batch size) pairs. As compute grows, the basin slides: bigger batches, smaller learning rates, along a straight line in log-log space. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Model scale M = non-embedding FLOPs per token = 72 * n_layer * d_model^2 + 12 * n_layer * d_model * l_seq. Compute C = M * D. Fitted laws (verify the constants in Section 3 of the paper): eta_opt = 0.3118 * C^(-0.1250) and B_opt = 0.2920 * C^(0.3271), with B in tokens. Optimal allocation M_opt = 0.1715 * C^0.5243 and D_opt = 5.8316 * C^0.4757. Why M and not N: 6N ignores attention FLOPs, which matter for small models with long context.

5:00 CODE — scaling_hparams.py: flops_per_token(n_layer, d_model, seq) implements M. grid_runs(budgets=[1e15, 3e15, 1e16, 3e16]) trains my M06 GPT on TinyStories at 4 compute budgets, each with a grid of 5 learning rates by 4 batch sizes, using a warmup-stable-decay schedule like the paper's multi-step schedule. For each budget, collect all configs within 0.25 percent of the best loss (the paper's 'near-optimal' band). fit_power_law(C, values) with np.polyfit on log-log.

8:30 RECEIPT — Receipt one: flops_per_token for a GPT-2 small config matches a measured count from torch.utils.flop_counter.FlopCounterMode divided by 3 for forward only, within 5 percent. Receipt two: plot my fitted eta_opt and B_opt exponents next to DeepSeek's -0.125 and 0.327. At 1e15 to 3e16 FLOPs the constants will differ, but the signs and rough slopes should agree, and I report whether they do.
10:30 MEASURE — Two log-log plots: near-optimal (B, eta) points per budget with my fit and the paper's fit overlaid. A third plot: loss vs learning rate at one budget, showing how flat the basin is.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Fit hyperparameters on small runs, express them as power laws in compute, and extrapolate. Interview line: optimal batch size grows and learning rate shrinks with compute, and DeepSeek measured model size in non-embedding FLOPs per token so attention cost counts.
12:45 NEXT — Next: DeepSeekMoE: fine-grained and shared experts
key_math: M = 72 n_layer d^2 + 12 n_layer d l_seq; C = M D; eta_opt = 0.3118 C^-0.1250; B_opt = 0.2920 C^0.3271 (verify constants in the paper).
code_task: flops_per_token(n_layer, d_model, seq_len) -> float; train_run(lr, batch_tokens, flops_budget) -> final_val_loss using the M06E09 GPT and a WSD schedule; near_optimal(results, tol=0.0025) -> list of (C, B, lr); fit_power_law(C: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> (coef, exponent).
receipt: abs(flops_per_token(12, 768, 1024) * 3 - measured_flops_per_token_fwd_bwd) / measured < 0.05 using FlopCounterMode; fitted exponents plotted beside DeepSeek's (-0.125 for lr, +0.327 for batch) with signs matching.
gotchas: Counting a run as near-optimal using the noisy final step instead of an averaged final loss makes the fit jump around, average the last few evals; batch size in sequences vs tokens changes the constant by seq_len, the paper uses tokens; tiny budgets saturate on TinyStories so the slope flattens, keep the budgets where loss still drops.
interview_q: How would you choose the learning rate and batch size for a run you can only afford once? Run a grid at several small compute budgets, take the near-optimal configs, fit power laws for lr and batch size against compute, and extrapolate to the target budget, as DeepSeek LLM did.
explainer: Here is a grid of training runs. Learning rate across, batch size up, and each square's color is its final loss.
There is no single best point. There is a wide pale basin where everything is within a quarter percent of the best.
Now we redo the grid with ten times more compute. The basin slides up and to the left.
Bigger batches, smaller learning rates. We mark the center of the basin at each compute budget.
On a log-log plot those centers line up. Two straight lines, one for batch size and one for learning rate.
The slopes are the exponents. DeepSeek measured about plus a third for batch size and minus an eighth for learning rate.
Our tiny runs give our own slopes, and we overlay them on DeepSeek's lines to see if they agree.

hook: Split 16 experts into 64 smaller ones and the number of possible expert combinations goes from 120 to over four billion.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Split 16 experts into 64 smaller ones and the number of possible expert combinations goes from 120 to over four billion.

0:15 QUESTION — GShard and Mixtral route each token to 2 of 8 or 16 big experts. DeepSeekMoE argued that this forces each expert to learn a mix of unrelated knowledge, and that every expert wastes capacity relearning common patterns. Its fix, fine-grained plus shared experts, is the MoE layer inside V2, V3 and V4.

1:00 INTUITION — Two moves. Fine-grained segmentation: cut each big expert into m smaller ones and route to m times as many, same FLOPs, far more combinations, so experts can specialize. Shared experts: a few experts every token always uses, so common knowledge lives there once instead of in every routed expert. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Output: h_t = u_t + sum_{i=1}^{K_s} FFN_i(u_t) + sum_{i=K_s+1}^{mN} g_{i,t} FFN_i(u_t). Gate: s_{i,t} = softmax_i(u_t^T e_i), g_{i,t} = s_{i,t} if s_{i,t} in TopK(mK - K_s) else 0. Each fine-grained expert has hidden size d_ff / m, so FLOPs per token stay equal to top-K of N big experts. Combinations: C(16, 2) = 120 vs C(64, 8) = 4,426,165,368. Expert balance loss: L_bal = alpha * sum_i f_i P_i, where f_i is the scaled fraction of tokens routed to i and P_i the mean gate prob.

5:00 CODE — class Expert(nn.Module): SwiGLU with hidden d_ff // m. class DeepSeekMoE(nn.Module) with shared: nn.ModuleList of K_s experts, routed: nn.ModuleList of m*N experts, gate: nn.Linear(d, m*N, bias=False). forward(x: (B, T, d)): flatten to (BT, d), scores = softmax(gate(x)), topk_vals, topk_idx = scores.topk(k), loop over experts with index_select, scatter_add outputs weighted by gate values. Add shared outputs. Baseline: plain top-2 of 8 with d_ff full width. Train both on TinyStories at equal active FLOPs and equal total params.

8:30 RECEIPT — Receipt one: with K_s=0, m=1 and k=N (every expert active), my layer equals a weighted sum of dense FFNs computed directly, assert_close at 1e-5. Receipt two: my routed output matches Hugging Face's DeepseekV2MoE-style reference on the same weights for a random batch (load one V2-Lite MoE layer with trust_remote_code on Mac, copy weights, assert_close in fp32). Receipt three, the published claim: the paper reports DeepSeekMoE 2B roughly matching GShard 2.9B; I check the direction of that result at 50M scale.

10:30 MEASURE — Val loss curves for top-2-of-8, fine-grained top-8-of-32, and fine-grained plus 1 shared, at matched active FLOPs, 3 seeds each with the band shaded. Expert load histogram for each. Then remove the shared expert at eval time and show the loss jump, the paper's evidence that shared experts hold common knowledge.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — More, smaller experts give routing more combinations, and shared experts stop every routed expert from relearning the basics. Interview line: fine-grained segmentation keeps FLOPs constant while raising combinatorial flexibility, and shared experts isolate common knowledge.
12:45 NEXT — Next: Building a DeepSeek-V2-Lite style block
key_math: h_t = u_t + sum_{i<=K_s} FFN_i(u_t) + sum_{i>K_s} g_{i,t} FFN_i(u_t); g = s if s in TopK(mK - K_s) else 0; C(64,8) = 4,426,165,368 vs C(16,2) = 120; L_bal = alpha sum_i f_i P_i.
code_task: Expert(d, d_ff_small) SwiGLU; DeepSeekMoE(d=512, n_routed=32, n_shared=1, top_k=7, d_ff_small=d_ff//4) with forward(x: (B,T,d)) -> (y: (B,T,d), aux_loss); routing via gate logits (BT, n_routed), topk (BT, k), token-to-expert dispatch with index_select and index_add_.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(my_moe(x), hf_moe_layer(x), rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-4) with weights copied from one DeepSeek-V2-Lite MoE layer in fp32; all-experts-active case equals explicit weighted sum of dense FFNs.
gotchas: Softmax then top-k vs top-k then softmax give different gate values, V2 uses softmax over all then top-k without renormalization (check norm_topk_prob in the config); looping over experts in Python is slow but correct, profile before optimizing; matching total params instead of active FLOPs makes the comparison unfair to the baseline.
interview_q: Why does DeepSeekMoE use many small experts plus shared experts instead of a few large experts? Fine-grained experts raise the number of routing combinations at constant FLOPs so experts specialize, and shared experts absorb common knowledge so routed experts do not duplicate it.
explainer: Here is a classic MoE layer. Eight big experts, and each token is sent to the best two.
Now we cut every expert into four slices. Thirty two small experts, and each token goes to eight of them.
The math per token is the same. But the number of ways to pick experts explodes from a hundred twenty to billions.
With more combinations, each small expert can focus on something narrow, like code indentation or dates.
There is still knowledge every token needs, like basic grammar. Without help, every expert learns a copy of it.
So we add one shared expert that every token always passes through. Common knowledge lives there once.
Turn the shared expert off at test time and the loss jumps. That is the evidence it really holds the basics.

yt_title: DeepSeekMoE from Scratch: Fine-Grained and Shared Experts in PyTorch
x_post: DeepSeekMoE: split each expert into 4 smaller ones and route to 4x as many. Same FLOPs per token, but C(64,8)=4.4B routing combos vs C(16,2)=120. Plus one always-on shared expert for common knowledge. Code + video:
linkedin: I built a DeepSeekMoE layer from scratch and checked it against a real DeepSeek-V2-Lite MoE layer with copied weights. At small scale, fine-grained experts plus a shared expert beat plain top-2 MoE at equal active FLOPs, across 3 seeds. Disabling the shared expert at eval time made the loss jump.

hook: A Llama block caches 4096 numbers per token per layer. The DeepSeek-V2-Lite block caches 576 and still has 16 heads.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — A Llama block caches 4096 numbers per token per layer. The DeepSeek-V2-Lite block caches 576 and still has 16 heads.

0:15 QUESTION — DeepSeek-V2 put MLA and DeepSeekMoE in one block and reported a 93.3 percent smaller KV cache and 5.76x higher max generation throughput than DeepSeek 67B. V2-Lite is the small version, 15.7B total and about 2.4B active, small enough to load layer by layer on a Mac. We build its block and check every parameter.

1:00 INTUITION — Two compressions in one block. Attention compresses keys and values into one small latent vector per token, plus a small shared RoPE key. The MLP compresses compute: 64 routed experts, 6 active, plus 2 shared. Memory goes down in attention, FLOPs go down in the MLP. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — MLA (from M09E04): c_KV = W_DKV h, with d_c = 512. k_C = W_UK c_KV, v = W_UV c_KV. Decoupled RoPE key k_R = RoPE(W_KR h) with d_R = 64, shared across heads. Query in V2-Lite is not compressed: q = W_Q h, split into q_C and q_R. Cache per token per layer: d_c + d_R = 576 elements. Llama-style MHA with 16 heads of 128: 2 * 16 * 128 = 4096. GQA with 4 KV heads: 1024. Params: count W_DKV (2048 x 576 including the RoPE key), W_UK and W_UV (512 x 16*128 each), W_Q, W_O, and the MoE experts. Verify every dimension against the V2-Lite config.json.

5:00 CODE — Read config.json of deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite: hidden_size, num_attention_heads, kv_lora_rank, qk_rope_head_dim, qk_nope_head_dim, v_head_dim, n_routed_experts, n_shared_experts, num_experts_per_tok, moe_intermediate_size, first_k_dense_replace. class MLA(nn.Module) and reuse DeepSeekMoE from M15E03. class V2LiteBlock: x = x + MLA(RMSNorm(x)); x = x + MoE(RMSNorm(x)). Load one layer's weights from the safetensors shard with safetensors.safe_open, map names, load_state_dict(strict=True).

8:30 RECEIPT — Receipt one: strict=True load succeeds, which proves every parameter shape matches. Receipt two: my block's output equals the reference DeepSeek-V2-Lite decoder layer from trust_remote_code on the same hidden states and positions, assert_close in fp32 at 1e-4. Receipt three: sum(p.numel()) for my block equals the reference layer's count.

10:30 MEASURE — Table: Llama-style MHA, GQA-4, MLA, each with params per attention layer and KV bytes per token per layer in bf16, then KV cache in GB at 32k context for the full 27-layer model. MLA: 576 * 2 bytes * 27 layers is about 31 KB per token. Bar chart of the same.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — The V2 block cuts memory with latent attention and cuts compute with fine-grained MoE, and both are checkable to the parameter. Interview line: MLA caches one 512-dim latent plus a 64-dim RoPE key per token per layer, independent of head count.
12:45 NEXT — Next: Multi-token prediction (DeepSeek-V3)
key_math: c_KV = W_DKV h (d_c=512); k_C = W_UK c_KV; v = W_UV c_KV; k_R = RoPE(W_KR h) (d_R=64); cache/token/layer = d_c + d_R = 576 vs MHA 2 n_h d_h = 4096.
code_task: MLA(d=2048, n_heads=16, d_c=512, d_nope=128, d_rope=64, d_v=128) with forward(h: (B,T,2048), pos) -> (B,T,2048) and a cache of (B,T,576); V2LiteBlock(config) combining MLA and DeepSeekMoE; load_layer(path, idx) maps safetensors keys to my module names.
receipt: block.load_state_dict(ref_layer_state, strict=True) succeeds; torch.testing.assert_close(my_block(h, pos), ref_layer(h, position_ids=pos)[0], rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-4) in fp32; parameter counts equal.
gotchas: The first layer of V2-Lite is dense (first_k_dense_replace), so loading layer 0 into an MoE block fails, use layer 1 or later; the RoPE key part uses a different rotary layout (interleaved vs half split) than Llama in some implementations, check the reference apply_rotary_pos_emb; the reference applies a softmax scale with YaRN mscale for long context, include it or outputs differ slightly.
interview_q: How much KV cache does MLA save relative to MHA and GQA? Per token per layer, MLA caches d_c + d_R (512 + 64 = 576 values) regardless of head count, versus 2 n_h d_h for MHA (4096 for 16 heads of 128) and 2 n_kv d_h for GQA.
explainer: Here is one DeepSeek-V2-Lite block. Attention on the left, the mixture of experts on the right, a residual stream through both.
In attention, each token's hidden state is squeezed into a single five hundred twelve number latent.
Keys and values for all sixteen heads are rebuilt from that latent when needed. Only the latent is cached.
Position needs special care, so a small sixty four number rotary key rides alongside the latent.
Five hundred seventy six numbers per token per layer. A Llama style block with the same heads stores four thousand ninety six.
On the right, the token visits six of sixty four routed experts and both shared experts.
We load real V2-Lite weights into our block, and the output matches the reference to four decimals.

hook: DeepSeek-V3 trains a second prediction head for the token after next. At inference, that head drafts tokens for free.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — DeepSeek-V3 trains a second prediction head for the token after next. At inference, that head drafts tokens for free.

0:15 QUESTION — DeepSeek-V3 adds multi-token prediction: one extra sequential module predicts token t+2 from the main model's hidden state and the embedding of token t+1. It densifies the training signal, and the report says the MTP head's second-token acceptance rate is 85 to 90 percent, giving about 1.8x decoding speed. This is the last architecture piece P6 needs before training.

1:00 INTUITION — The main model makes a guess for the next word. A small helper looks at what the main model was thinking plus the real next word and guesses one word further. Unlike Gloeckle et al.'s parallel heads, the helper is chained, so the causal story stays intact. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — For depth k: h'_i^k = M_k [ RMSNorm(h_i^(k-1)) ; RMSNorm(Emb(t_(i+k))) ], with M_k of shape (d, 2d). h^k = TRM_k(h'^k), one transformer block. P_(i+k+1)^k = OutHead(h_i^k), with the embedding and output head shared with the main model. L_MTP^k = CE over positions. Total: L = L_main + (lambda / D) * sum_k L_MTP^k. V3 uses D = 1, lambda = 0.3 for the first 10T tokens then 0.1 (verify in the V3 report, section 2.2). At inference, drop the MTP module or use it as the draft model for speculative decoding.

5:00 CODE — class MTPModule(nn.Module) with norm_h, norm_e (RMSNorm), proj: nn.Linear(2d, d, bias=False), block: TransformerBlock. forward(h_main: (B,T,d), next_emb: (B,T,d)) -> h_mtp (B,T,d). In GPT.forward: logits = head(h); emb_shift = embed(tokens[:, 1:]); h_mtp = mtp(h[:, :-1], emb_shift); mtp_logits = head(h_mtp); loss_mtp = CE(mtp_logits[:, :-1], tokens[:, 2:]). At inference the main head picks the next token. The helper drafts the one after it, for almost no cost.
One forward pass checks the draft. If it matches, we got two tokens for one step.

hook: Hopper's FP8 tensor cores accumulate with limited precision. DeepSeek fixed it by copying partial sums to FP32 every 128 elements.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Hopper's FP8 tensor cores accumulate with limited precision. DeepSeek fixed it by copying partial sums to FP32 every 128 elements.

0:15 QUESTION — DeepSeek-V3 is one of the first open models of its size trained mostly in FP8, and the report says the relative loss error stayed below 0.25 percent vs BF16. Two tricks made it work: fine-grained scaling so one outlier does not crush a whole tensor, and promoting accumulation to FP32. P6 trains in FP8, so we build both and measure them on an H100.

1:00 INTUITION — FP8 E4M3 has only about 448 of headroom and 3 mantissa bits. A per-tensor scale is one volume knob for a whole orchestra: one loud outlier forces everyone else into silence. Per-tile scales give each small group its own knob. And long dot products drift in low-precision accumulators, so every 128 elements you hand the running total to FP32. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Activation tiles 1x128: s_a = max|A[i, 128j:128(j+1)]| / 448, A_fp8 = round_e4m3(A / s_a). Weight blocks 128x128: s_w = max|W_block| / 448. GEMM: C[i,n] = sum_j s_a[i,j] * s_w[j,n_block] * sum_{k in tile j} A_fp8[i,k] W_fp8[k,n]. The inner sum runs on tensor cores; the scale multiply and FP32 accumulate happen per K-tile of 128 on CUDA cores, which is the promotion interval N_C = 128. V3 uses E4M3 for all tensors, including gradients, thanks to the fine-grained scaling (verify in section 3.3 of the report).

5:00 CODE — On RunPod 1x H100. quant_tile(x: (M,K)) -> (x_fp8: float8_e4m3fn (M,K), scale: float32 (M, K//128)). quant_block(w: (N,K)) -> (w_fp8, scale (N//128, K//128)). ref_fp8_gemm(a_fp8, a_s, w_fp8, w_s) in PyTorch: loop over K tiles, upcast each tile product to fp32, scale, accumulate. Fast paths: torch._scaled_mm for per-tensor scaling, and DeepGEMM's FP8 GEMM for block scaling (install from the repo; check the current function name in its README). Inject outliers: set 0.1 percent of activations to 100x.

Receipt two: relative error vs the fp32 matmul for per-tensor vs tile-wise scaling with outliers: tile-wise should be clearly lower. Receipt three: accumulate an fp8 product over K=16384 without promotion (simulated low-precision accumulator) and show the error grows with K, then flat with promotion every 128.

interview_q: Why does DeepSeek-V3 use fine-grained FP8 scaling instead of per-tensor scaling? Activation outliers force a per-tensor scale so large that most values underflow in E4M3; 1x128 tile and 128x128 block scales confine an outlier's damage to its own tile, and FP32 promotion every 128 K-elements fixes limited tensor-core accumulation precision.
explainer: Here is a matrix of activations as a grid of colored cells. A few cells in one row are a hundred times larger than the rest.
With one scale for the whole tensor, the big cells set the range. Everything else rounds to almost zero in FP8.
Now we cut each row into tiles of one hundred twenty eight. Each tile gets its own scale.
The outlier only ruins its own tile. Every other tile uses the full FP8 range.
Weights get square blocks of one twenty eight by one twenty eight, each with its own scale too.
Inside the matmul, tensor cores add up FP8 products with limited precision. Over thousands of terms, error builds.
So every one hundred twenty eight terms we move the running sum into a full FP32 register. The error curve goes flat.

hook: In DeepSeek-V3, cross-node expert communication costs roughly as much time as compute. DualPipe hides it.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — In DeepSeek-V3, cross-node expert communication costs roughly as much time as compute. DualPipe hides it.

0:15 QUESTION — With expert parallelism across nodes, every MoE layer does an all-to-all dispatch and combine. The V3 report says this pushed the computation-to-communication ratio to about 1:1. DualPipe feeds micro-batches from both ends of the pipeline and overlaps one micro-batch's communication with another's compute. It is open-sourced as deepseek-ai/DualPipe.

1:00 INTUITION — 1F1B is a one-way assembly line, so the first and last stations sit idle at the start and end. DualPipe runs two assembly lines in opposite directions on the same stations. While one batch waits for the network, the station works on a batch coming the other way. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Bubble sizes from the DualPipe README (verify there): 1F1B: (PP - 1)(F + B). ZB1P: (PP - 1)(F + B - 2W). DualPipe: (PP/2 - 1)(F&B + B - 3W), where F is forward chunk time, B full backward, W the weight-gradient part of backward, F&B two mutually overlapped forward and backward chunks. Cost: DualPipe keeps 2x parameter copies per stage and PP + 1 activation memory. Each chunk splits into attention, all-to-all dispatch, MLP, all-to-all combine, and the backward splits into input-grad and weight-grad, so the scheduler can slot communication under compute.

hook: If one GPU holds the experts everyone wants, the other GPUs in the step wait for it. EPLB copies the popular experts.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — If one GPU holds the experts everyone wants, the other GPUs in the step wait for it. EPLB copies the popular experts.

0:15 QUESTION — In expert parallelism, each GPU owns some experts and tokens travel to them by all-to-all. DeepSeek open-sourced DeepEP, the kernels that move tokens, and EPLB, the algorithm that decides where experts live and which ones get duplicated. Together they decide whether V3-scale MoE runs at full speed or at the speed of its busiest GPU.

1:00 INTUITION — Experts are checkout lanes and tokens are shoppers. A few lanes are always popular. EPLB opens extra copies of the popular lanes and spreads lanes across stores (nodes) so no store gets slammed. DeepEP is the conveyor belt that moves shoppers to lanes, with a fast path for NVLink inside a node and RDMA across nodes. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Load per GPU g: L_g = sum_{e on g} load_e / replicas_e. Imbalance = max_g L_g / mean_g L_g, and step time is set by the max. EPLB: given expert loads and R redundant slots, assign replicas to the heaviest experts (greedy on load per replica), then pack replicas onto GPUs with balanced bin-packing. Hierarchical mode: first pack expert groups onto nodes (to keep V3's node-limited routing, at most 4 nodes per token), then replicate within nodes, then pack onto GPUs. Global mode ignores groups, used for decoding with larger EP.

5:00 CODE — pip install from deepseek-ai/EPLB (it is a single Python file). Build a skewed load trace: Zipf with exponent 1.2 over 256 experts, or log expert counts from my M15E03 MoE on TinyStories. Read DeepEP's README: normal kernels for training and prefill, low-latency kernels for decoding, and the dispatch/combine API.

hook: FlashMLA claims about 3000 GB per second on decode. On an H100 I measured mine, and the gap is the lesson.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — FlashMLA claims about 3000 GB per second on decode. On an H100 I measured mine, and the gap is the lesson.

0:15 QUESTION — FlashMLA and DeepGEMM were the first two repos of DeepSeek's open-source week. FlashMLA is the MLA decode kernel; its README reports up to 3000 GB/s in the memory-bound setting and about 580 TFLOPs compute-bound on H800 (verify current numbers, later versions report higher). DeepGEMM is a compact FP8 GEMM library with fine-grained scaling. Reading them is a masterclass in Hopper.

1:00 INTUITION — MLA decode reads a small shared latent cache and multiplies it by many query heads, so it behaves more like a GEMM than a GEMV. FlashMLA keeps the latent in shared memory, splits long sequences across thread blocks, and uses Hopper's async copy engine (TMA) and warpgroup matmuls (WGMMA) so loading and math overlap. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Bytes per decode step for one sequence of length L in one layer: L * (512 + 64) * 2 bytes for the bf16 latent and RoPE key. Achieved bandwidth = total bytes / time. Arithmetic intensity: with absorbed weights, each cached latent is used by all n_h query heads, so FLOPs = 2 * n_h * L * (576 + 512) against L * 1152 bytes, an intensity of about 1.9 * n_h FLOPs per byte. With 128 heads that is about 240, right at the H100 ridge point of roughly 295 FLOPs/byte (989 TFLOPs / 3.35 TB/s), and with two query tokens per step (MTP) it is past it. That is why FlashMLA reports both a memory-bound and a compute-bound number.

5:00 CODE — On RunPod 1x H100. Clone FlashMLA, pip install. Use get_mla_metadata and flash_mla_with_kvcache with a paged cache of block size 64 (check the current test script for exact arguments). Write mla_decode_ref(q: (B, 1, 128, 576), kv_cache: (B, L, 1, 576), v_dim=512) in PyTorch: scores = q @ k^T * scale, softmax, out = p @ kv[..., :512]. Then annotate the kernel: tile loop, TMA loads, the split-KV combine step. Then DeepGEMM: point to the JIT-compiled kernel, the scale promotion on CUDA cores, and the persistent warp-specialized structure.

8:30 RECEIPT — Receipt one: torch.testing.assert_close(flash_mla_out, mla_decode_ref(q, cache), atol=2e-3, rtol=2e-3) in bf16 for batch 64, L in {1k, 4k, 16k}. Receipt two: achieved bandwidth from my bytes/time formula compared to the README's number; on H100 SXM with about 3.35 TB/s peak HBM3 I expect to land within 10 to 20 percent of what the README reports for H800 in the memory-bound case.

Interview line: with absorbed weights, MLA decode reuses each cached latent across all query heads, giving arithmetic intensity proportional to head count.

interview_q: Why is MLA decode less memory-bound than GQA decode? With weight absorption every query head attends directly over the same compressed latent, so each cached byte is reused by all heads; the arithmetic intensity scales with head count instead of being about 1 FLOP per byte.
explainer: Here is decode for one token. One query row per head, and a long cache of latents behind it.
In ordinary attention each head has its own keys, so every byte of cache is used once. That is memory-bound.
In MLA all one hundred twenty eight heads read the same latent. Each byte loaded is used one hundred twenty eight times.
So the kernel lives on both sides of the roofline. It needs fast loads and fast math at the same time.
FlashMLA tiles the cache, streams tiles into shared memory with Hopper's copy engine, and multiplies while the next tile loads.
For very long sequences it splits the cache across thread blocks, then merges partial softmaxes at the end.
Our PyTorch reference gets the same answer. FlashMLA gets it many times faster, close to the hardware roof.

hook: R1-Zero went from 15.6 to 71.0 percent on AIME with no supervised data, just a correctness check and GRPO.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — R1-Zero went from 15.6 to 71.0 percent on AIME with no supervised data, just a correctness check and GRPO.

0:15 QUESTION — DeepSeek-R1 showed that reasoning can emerge from reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards on a strong base model. Then it added four stages to make the model usable and distilled it into small Qwen and Llama models. I already built SFT, GRPO and distillation in M11. Today I map the whole recipe onto that code, and check a published number.

1:00 INTUITION — R1-Zero is a talented student given only an answer key: it learns to think longer, but its notes are messy and switch languages. R1 first shows the student a few thousand clean worked examples, then runs RL, then keeps the student's best answers as a new textbook, then runs RL again. Distillation hands that textbook to smaller students. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — GRPO (M11E11): for each prompt sample G outputs, advantage A_i = (r_i - mean(r)) / std(r), objective = mean_i min(rho_i A_i, clip(rho_i, 1-eps, 1+eps) A_i) - beta KL(pi || pi_ref). R1-Zero reward = accuracy reward (rule-checked answer) + format reward (thinking inside tags). R1 adds a language consistency reward in reasoning RL. Rejection sampling: generate many, keep correct and readable ones, about 600k reasoning and 200k non-reasoning samples for SFT (verify counts in the paper). Distillation is plain SFT on those 800k samples, no RL.

5:00 CODE — r1_pipeline.py: a diagram where each stage points to my code. Stage 0, base model. Stage 1, cold-start SFT: sft_train from M11E03 on a few thousand long CoT samples. Stage 2, reasoning RL: grpo_step from M11E12 with reward = accuracy + format + language consistency. Stage 3, rejection sampling: sample_n(model, prompts, n=16), filter with the verifier, build SFT set. Stage 4, SFT on that set plus general data, then a second RL stage for helpfulness and harmlessness. Stage 5, distill: SFT a small student. Run stage 3 and stage 5 at toy scale on GSM8K with Qwen2.5-0.5B on my Mac.

8:30 RECEIPT — Evaluate DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on MATH-500 with the paper's sampling settings (temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95) using vLLM on a rented GPU or a 100-problem subset on Mac. Compare pass@1 to the paper's reported 83.9 for this model (verify in the distillation table). My number should be within a few points given fewer samples per problem; I report the CI from M14E04.

10:30 MEASURE — Histogram of response lengths for the distilled 1.5B vs the base Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B on the same problems. Accuracy vs max generation length (2k, 4k, 8k, 16k tokens): truncation costs accuracy, which is why R1 models need long budgets.

Interview line: R1-Zero proved reasoning can emerge from pure RL, while R1's cold start and rejection sampling fixed readability, and distillation transferred it to small models better than RL on them directly.

hook: DeepSeek-V3.2 lets each token attend to only 2048 of the previous 128,000. A tiny ReLU indexer picks which ones.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — DeepSeek-V3.2 lets each token attend to only 2048 of the previous 128,000. A tiny ReLU indexer picks which ones.

0:15 QUESTION — DeepSeek-V3.2 introduced DeepSeek Sparse Attention: a lightning indexer scores every previous token cheaply, and the main MLA attention runs only on the top 2048. The paper says this cuts core attention from O(L^2) to O(Lk) while matching V3.1-Terminus quality. It is also the seed of V4's attention, and one of the ablations in P6.

1:00 INTUITION — A librarian with a card catalog. Before reading every book in a 128k-book library, you flip through a cheap index and pull the 2048 most relevant. The index costs O(L^2) too, but each comparison is tiny, few heads, small dims, FP8, ReLU instead of softmax. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Index score (eq. 1 of the V3.2 paper): I_{t,s} = sum_{j=1}^{H^I} w_{t,j}^I * ReLU(q_{t,j}^I . k_s^I). Selection (eq. 2): u_t = Attn(h_t, { c_s : I_{t,s} in TopK(I_{t,:}) }), k = 2048. Training stage 1, dense warm-up: freeze everything but the indexer and minimize L^I = sum_t KL( p_{t,:} || softmax(I_{t,:}) ), where p is the main attention summed over heads and L1-normalized (1000 steps, 16 x 128k sequences, about 2.1B tokens). Stage 2, sparse training: train all parameters, detach the indexer input, KL only over the selected set S_t (15,000 steps, about 943.7B tokens). DSA is implemented on the MQA mode of MLA so one selected latent serves all query heads. H^I is not stated in the paper text; the released config lists the indexer head count and dims (verify there).

6:00 CODE — On RunPod 1x RTX 4090. class LightningIndexer(nn.Module): wq: Linear(d, H_I * d_I), wk: Linear(d, d_I), ww: Linear(d, H_I); forward(h: (B,T,d)) -> I: (B,T,T) = einsum('bthd,bsd->bths', q, k).relu() weighted by w and summed over h, causal-masked to -inf. class DSAAttention: idx = I.topk(k, dim=-1).indices -> (B,T,k); gather K and V rows -> (B,T,k,d_h); attend with softmax over k. Warm-up loss: target = attention probs from the dense model summed over heads, normalized; F.kl_div(log_softmax(I), target). Start from my M06 GPT trained at 4k context, extend to 16k.

9:00 RECEIPT — Receipt one: with k >= T, DSA output equals dense causal attention exactly: torch.testing.assert_close(dsa(x, k=T), F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)). Receipt two: after warm-up, top-k recall, the fraction of true attention mass inside the selected set, goes above 0.9 at k = T/8. Receipt three: the KL during warm-up falls monotonically, mirroring the paper's two-stage recipe.

11:00 MEASURE — Plot: val loss at 16k context for dense, DSA k=2048, DSA k=512, and a random top-k baseline. Second plot: attention FLOPs and measured time per step vs context length. Be honest: my gather-based implementation is not a fused kernel, so FLOPs drop more than wall clock; point to FlashMLA's sparse kernels for the real speedup.

12:30 TAKEAWAY — DSA makes long-context attention cost O(Lk) by letting a cheap ReLU indexer choose which tokens deserve full attention, trained first to imitate dense attention. Interview line: the lightning indexer is still quadratic, but with few heads and FP8 it is much cheaper than MLA, and the main attention becomes linear in L for fixed k.
13:15 NEXT — Next: mHC: manifold-constrained hyper-connections
key_math: I_{t,s} = sum_{j=1}^{H^I} w^I_{t,j} ReLU(q^I_{t,j} . k^I_s); u_t = Attn(h_t, {c_s | I_{t,s} in TopK(I_{t,:})}), k = 2048; warm-up L^I = sum_t KL(p_{t,:} || softmax(I_{t,:})); sparse L^I = sum_t KL(p_{t,S_t} || softmax(I_{t,S_t})).
code_task: LightningIndexer(d, n_heads_idx=4, d_idx=64) -> scores (B,T,T) with causal mask; DSAAttention(d, n_heads, topk) -> gathers K,V at topk indices (B,T,k,d_h) and attends; warmup_loss(index_scores, dense_attn_probs (B,H,T,T)) -> KL; topk_recall(dense_probs, idx) -> float.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(dsa_attn(x, topk=T), F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True), atol=1e-5, rtol=1e-5) in fp32; top-k recall of dense attention mass > 0.9 at k = T/8 after warm-up; warm-up KL decreasing.
gotchas: For early positions t < k there are fewer than k valid tokens, so top-k picks masked -inf entries unless you clamp k to t+1 or mask afterward; materializing the full (B,T,T) index matrix at 16k is 1 GB per sequence in fp32, chunk over queries; forgetting to detach the indexer input in stage 2 lets the KL loss reshape the main model.
interview_q: How does DeepSeek Sparse Attention reduce long-context cost if the indexer is still O(L^2)? The indexer uses few heads, small dimensions, ReLU and FP8, so its quadratic term is far cheaper than MLA's; the expensive main attention only processes k = 2048 selected tokens per query, making it O(Lk).
explainer: Here is one query token at position one hundred thousand, and every earlier token stretching out behind it.
Full attention compares the query against all of them, with every head, at full precision. That is expensive.
The lightning indexer does a cheap pass first. A few small heads, a ReLU, and a weighted sum give one score per earlier token.
We keep the top two thousand forty eight scores. Only those tokens go into real attention.
How does the indexer learn what matters? At first it copies the dense model's attention pattern, measured with KL divergence.
Then the model trains with sparse attention switched on, and the indexer keeps tracking the selected tokens.
With k equal to the full length, the sparse output matches dense attention exactly. That is our first check.

hook: Hyper-connections widen the residual stream and gain accuracy, but DeepSeek measured signal gains up to 3000x. Sinkhorn fixed it.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Hyper-connections widen the residual stream and gain accuracy, but DeepSeek measured signal gains up to 3000x. Sinkhorn fixed it.

0:15 QUESTION — Hyper-connections (Zhu et al. 2024) replace the single residual stream with n parallel streams and learned mixing. DeepSeek's mHC paper (arXiv 2512.24880) found that unconstrained mixing breaks the identity mapping and causes loss surges at scale. Their fix constrains the mixing matrix to be doubly stochastic. mHC then shipped in DeepSeek-V4 with n = 4. It is one of P6's ablations.

1:00 INTUITION — A residual connection is a pipe that carries the signal unchanged. Hyper-connections use four pipes and let each layer remix them. If the remix can amplify, after 60 layers a small amplification compounds into an explosion. A doubly stochastic matrix only averages, every row and column sums to one, so the products of many of them stay bounded. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — HC propagation: x_{l+1} = H_res,l x_l + H_post,l^T F(H_pre,l x_l, W_l), with x_l in R^(n x C), n = 4. mHC dynamic mappings: x' = RMSNorm(vec(x_l)), H~_pre = alpha_pre (x' phi_pre) + b_pre, same for post and res. Constraints (eq. 8): H_pre = sigmoid(H~_pre), H_post = 2 sigmoid(H~_post), H_res = SinkhornKnopp(H~_res). Sinkhorn: M^(0) = exp(H~_res), then alternate row and column normalization, t_max = 20. Doubly stochastic means H 1 = 1, 1^T H = 1^T, H >= 0, the Birkhoff polytope, which is closed under multiplication, so the composite over all layers is also doubly stochastic. Alpha initialized to 0.01. Paper results on 27B: HC gain magnitude peaks near 3000, mHC about 1.6; mHC beats HC on BBH by 2.1 points (51.0 vs 48.9) and on DROP by 2.3; overhead 6.7 percent at n = 4 with fused kernels.

6:00 CODE — sinkhorn(logits: (..., n, n), iters=20) -> doubly stochastic. class MHCBlock(nn.Module): wraps an attention or MLP sublayer F. Params phi_pre (nC, n), phi_post (nC, n), phi_res (nC, n*n), b_pre, b_post, b_res, alpha_* = 0.01. forward(x: (B, T, n, C)): xv = rms_norm(x.flatten(-2)); h_pre = sigmoid(alpha_pre * xv @ phi_pre + b_pre) -> (B,T,n); layer_in = einsum('btn,btnc->btc', h_pre, x); y = F(layer_in); h_post = 2 * sigmoid(...); h_res = sinkhorn(...) -> (B,T,n,n); x_next = einsum('btij,btjc->btic', h_res, x) + h_post[..., None] * y[..., None, :]. Three variants of my M06 GPT: residual, HC (tanh-based, unconstrained), mHC. Track loss and the gain magnitude of the composite H_res product.

9:00 RECEIPT — Receipt one: sinkhorn output has row and column sums within 1e-3 of 1 after 20 iterations and all entries positive. Receipt two: with n = 1 the mHC block reduces to x + 2 sigmoid(b) * F(sigmoid(b') x); fixing those gates to 1 gives exactly the standard residual block, assert_close against my M05 block. Receipt three: the product of H_res over all layers stays doubly stochastic, so its max row sum is 1 within 1e-2, while the HC product's max row sum grows during training. Compare the shape of that curve to the paper's gain-magnitude figure (verify its exact definition of Amax gain magnitude in the paper).

11:00 MEASURE — Plots over training steps for residual, HC and mHC, 3 seeds each: val loss, gradient norm, and composite gain magnitude. Table: final val loss and step time, with my unfused overhead vs the paper's 6.7 percent fused overhead.

12:30 TAKEAWAY — mHC keeps the benefit of a wider residual stream and restores stability by projecting the mixing matrix onto the doubly stochastic manifold with Sinkhorn. Interview line: doubly stochastic matrices are closed under multiplication, so the composite mapping across all layers cannot amplify the signal.
13:15 NEXT — Next: Engram: conditional memory as a new sparsity axis
key_math: x_{l+1} = H_res,l x_l + H_post,l^T F(H_pre,l x_l, W_l); H_pre = sigma(H~_pre), H_post = 2 sigma(H~_post), H_res = Sinkhorn(H~_res); Sinkhorn: M0 = exp(H~), M_t = T_r(T_c(M_{t-1})), t_max = 20; H1 = 1, 1^T H = 1^T, H >= 0.
code_task: sinkhorn(logits: (...,n,n), iters=20) -> (...,n,n); MHCBlock(sublayer, n=4, C=d_model) with forward(x: (B,T,n,C)) -> (B,T,n,C); HCBlock with unconstrained tanh mappings; GPT variant that expands the embedding to n streams at input and sums them at output; gain_magnitude(list of H_res) -> float (max abs row sum of the composite product).
receipt: assert torch.allclose(S.sum(-1), ones, atol=1e-3) and torch.allclose(S.sum(-2), ones, atol=1e-3) for S = sinkhorn(randn(4,4)); n=1 with gates fixed to 1 matches the standard pre-norm residual block via torch.testing.assert_close; composite mHC gain stays about 1 while HC's grows.
gotchas: Running Sinkhorn in bf16 drifts, do the exp and normalizations in fp32; exp of large logits overflows, subtract the max before exp; how the n streams are initialized from the embedding and collapsed at the output matters for loss at step 0, check the paper's choice and report yours.
interview_q: Why does mHC constrain the residual mixing matrix to be doubly stochastic? Unconstrained hyper-connection matrices compound across layers and can amplify signals by orders of magnitude, causing instability; doubly stochastic matrices have spectral norm at most 1 and are closed under multiplication, so the composite stays bounded and the identity-like behavior returns.
explainer: Here is a normal residual stream, one pipe running through every layer. Each layer adds its output, and the pipe carries the signal unchanged.
Hyper-connections widen it to four pipes. Before each layer, a small matrix mixes the four pipes together.
That mixing is learned, and nothing stops it from amplifying. A gain of one point one per layer becomes huge after sixty layers.
DeepSeek measured exactly this. The combined gain across layers spiked into the thousands, and the loss surged.
The fix is a constraint. Every row and every column of the mixing matrix must sum to one, with no negative entries.
Sinkhorn gets there by alternating. Normalize the rows, normalize the columns, twenty times, and it converges.
Multiply many of these matrices together and the result still has rows and columns summing to one. The gain stays near one.

hook: DeepSeek moved about a fifth of an MoE model's sparse parameters into a hashed N-gram lookup table, and reasoning scores went up.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — DeepSeek moved about a fifth of an MoE model's sparse parameters into a hashed N-gram lookup table, and reasoning scores went up.

0:15 QUESTION — The Engram paper (arXiv 2601.07372, code at github.com/deepseek-ai/Engram) argues transformers waste depth reconstructing static facts and phrases. It adds conditional memory: an O(1) hashed N-gram embedding lookup gated by the hidden state. At 27B total parameters and equal FLOPs, Engram beat a pure MoE baseline, with bigger gains on BBH (+5.0) than on knowledge tasks. Another P6 ablation.

1:00 INTUITION — MoE is conditional computation: pick which experts to run. Engram is conditional memory: pick which table rows to read. For a phrase like 'Alexander the Great', the model should look it up, not compute it over several layers. The gate lets the current context ignore a lookup that does not fit. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Tokenizer compression: map token ids through NFKC and lowercasing, about 23 percent fewer ids for a 128k vocab. Suffix N-gram g_{t,n} = (x'_{t-n+1}, ..., x'_t). For each order n and hash head k: z = phi_{n,k}(g_{t,n}) (multiplicative-XOR hash into a prime-sized table), e_{t,n,k} = E_{n,k}[z]. Concatenate all into e_t. Gate: k_t = W_K e_t, v_t = W_V e_t, alpha_t = sigmoid( RMSNorm(h_t)^T RMSNorm(k_t) / sqrt(d) ), v~_t = alpha_t v_t. Then Y = SiLU(Conv1D(RMSNorm(V~))) + V~ with kernel 4, and H <- H + Y. Allocation law: with rho the fraction of sparse params given to MoE experts, val loss is U-shaped in rho with an optimum near rho = 75 to 80 percent. Engram-27B: 5.7B Engram params, layers 2 and 15, N-grams up to 3, 8 heads.

6:00 CODE — On RunPod 1x RTX 4090. compress_ids(vocab) -> lookup tensor via unicodedata.normalize('NFKC', s).lower(). class Engram(nn.Module): tables nn.Embedding(M_{n,k}, d_e) for n in {2,3}, k in range(K); hash_ngram(ids: (B,T), n, k) -> (B,T) using rolling multiply-XOR mod prime; W_K, W_V: Linear; conv: nn.Conv1d(d, d, 4, groups=d, dilation=3, causal left-padding). forward(h: (B,T,d), ids: (B,T)) -> Y. Insert at layer 2 (and a later layer) of my M15E03 MoE GPT. Sweep rho in {100, 90, 80, 70, 50, 40} percent at fixed total and active params, 2 seeds each.

9:00 RECEIPT — Receipt one: with the gate forced to zero, the Engram model's output equals the backbone's exactly, assert_close. interview_q: What is the difference between conditional computation and conditional memory? MoE (conditional computation) chooses which parameters to compute with per token; Engram (conditional memory) chooses which embedding rows to read via a deterministic N-gram hash, which costs O(1) FLOPs and can be offloaded and prefetched because the address depends only on input tokens.
explainer: Here is a sentence entering the model, and one phrase in it: Alexander the Great.
A normal transformer rebuilds what that phrase means over several layers of computation, every time it sees it.
Engram looks at the last two and three tokens, hashes them, and reads matching rows from big embedding tables.
That lookup costs almost nothing. The address depends only on the tokens, so it can even be fetched ahead of time.
A gate compares the current hidden state with the retrieved memory. If the memory does not fit the context, the gate closes.
A short causal convolution smooths the result, and it is added back into the residual stream.
Now the budget question. Split sparse parameters between experts and memory, and the loss forms a U with its bottom near eighty percent experts.

hook: At one million tokens, DeepSeek-V4-Pro reports 10 percent of V3.2's KV cache. I rebuilt the calculator to check where that comes from.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — At one million tokens, DeepSeek-V4-Pro reports 10 percent of V3.2's KV cache. I rebuilt the calculator to check where that comes from.

0:15 QUESTION — DeepSeek-V4 (arXiv 2606.19348, April 2026) ships V4-Pro at 1.6T total and 49B active, and V4-Flash at 284B and 13B, both with 1M-token context. The abstract says V4-Pro needs 27 percent of the single-token inference FLOPs and 10 percent of the KV cache of V3.2 at 1M tokens. The new piece is hybrid attention: Compressed Sparse Attention and Heavily Compressed Attention. It also uses mHC and Muon.

1:00 INTUITION — V3.2 kept every token's latent and chose 2048 of them. V4 first compresses: CSA merges every 4 tokens into one KV entry and then sparsely selects among those; HCA merges every 128 tokens into one entry and attends to all of them densely. A 128-token sliding window keeps recent tokens exact. Cache shrinks by the compression rate. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — From the report (verify each against Section 2 and the config table): CSA compression m = 4, HCA m' = 128, sliding window n_win = 128, head dim c = 512 with shared-KV MQA, indexer 64 heads of dim 128, top-k 1024 for Pro and 512 for Flash. Compression: C_i = sum_j S_j * C_j over 2m overlapping entries, with S a softmax over learned weights plus positional bias, a learned weighted pool rather than a mean. KV cache precision: RoPE dims (64) in BF16, the rest in FP8. Per-layer bytes per token: CSA about (448 + 64*2)/4 = 144 bytes plus indexer keys; HCA about 576/128 = 4.5 bytes; SWA a constant 128 tokens. V3/V3.2 MLA: 576 elements, about 1152 bytes in BF16 (V3.2 adds indexer keys). Pro: 61 layers, first two HCA, rest interleaved CSA/HCA (verify the exact pattern).

6:00 CODE — kv_calc.py: dataclasses for V3 (MLA, 61 layers), V3.2 (MLA + indexer keys, top-k 2048) and V4-Pro (layer list of 'HCA'/'CSA'). kv_bytes_per_token(cfg, L) sums per layer. attn_flops_per_token(cfg, L): MLA dense 2 * n_h * L * (576 + 512) per layer for V3; V3.2 indexer 2 * H_I * d_I * L plus main attention over k; V4 CSA indexer over L/4 compressed entries plus attention over top-k plus window, HCA over L/128 entries plus window. Add MoE and projection FLOPs from active params (2 * N_active). Evaluate at L = 128k and 1M.

9:00 RECEIPT — The calculator must reproduce the report's headline: V4-Pro KV at 1M divided by V3.2 KV at 1M near 0.10, and single-token FLOPs ratio near 0.27. If I land at 0.06 or 0.15 instead, the beat is figuring out which assumption is off, layer pattern, indexer key precision, or whether the window cache counts, and I say on camera which detail I could not verify.

11:00 MEASURE — Stacked bar: KV GB per sequence at 128k and 1M for V3, V3.2, V4-Pro, V4-Flash, split into main cache, indexer cache, and window. Line plot: attention FLOPs per decoded token vs context length on log axes, V3 quadratic-in-total cost rising linearly per token, V4 nearly flat until the indexer term dominates.

12:30 TAKEAWAY — V4 reaches a million tokens by compressing the cache before selecting from it, 4x for sparse attention and 128x for dense global attention, with a small exact window for recent tokens. Interview line: CSA compresses KV 4x and runs a lightning-indexer top-k over the compressed entries, while HCA compresses 128x and attends densely, and they are interleaved.
13:15 NEXT — Next: DeepSeek-OCR and the infra papers
key_math: C_i = sum_{j in block i, 2m entries} softmax(Z_j + B_j) * C_j; CSA bytes/token/layer ~ (448*1 + 64*2)/4; HCA ~ 576/128; MLA ~ 576*2; FLOPs_attn,MLA ~ 2 n_h L (576+512) per layer per token.

receipt: kv_bytes(V4_Pro, 1M) / kv_bytes(V3_2, 1M) printed next to the report's 0.10, and flops_per_token(V4_Pro, 1M) / flops_per_token(V3_2, 1M) next to 0.27; any mismatch > 30% is traced to a named assumption marked 'verify in the paper'.
gotchas: Treating the SWA window as per-token cache double counts, it is a constant 128 tokens per layer; forgetting that V3.2's indexer keys are also cached understates V3.2 and makes V4 look better than reported; mixing elements and bytes (BF16 = 2, FP8 = 1, FP4 = 0.5) is the most common factor-of-two error.
interview_q: How does DeepSeek-V4 make 1M-token context affordable compared to V3.2? It compresses KV entries before attention: CSA pools every 4 tokens into one entry and selects top-k with a lightning indexer, HCA pools every 128 tokens and attends densely, plus a short exact sliding window, with FP8 cache storage, giving about 10% of V3.2's KV cache at 1M tokens.
explainer: Here is a million tokens of context as a long ribbon. V3.2 keeps one latent per token and picks the best two thousand.
V4 starts by compressing. In CSA layers, every four tokens are pooled into a single key value entry.
The pooling is learned. Each token gets a softmax weight, and neighboring blocks overlap a little.
A lightning indexer then picks the top thousand twenty four compressed entries for each query.
HCA layers compress much harder, one entry per hundred twenty eight tokens, and attend to all of them.
Both kinds also look at the last hundred twenty eight tokens exactly, so nearby detail is never blurred.
Add it up layer by layer and the cache at a million tokens is about a tenth of V3.2's.

hook: DeepSeek-OCR turns a page of text into 100 vision tokens and reads it back at about 97 percent precision. Text as pixels compresses.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — DeepSeek-OCR turns a page of text into 100 vision tokens and reads it back at about 97 percent precision. Text as pixels compresses.

0:15 QUESTION — DeepSeek-OCR (arXiv 2510.18234) asks a long-context question: can an image of text hold more information per token than the text itself? Its abstract reports about 97 percent decoding precision when text tokens are under 10x the vision tokens, and about 60 percent at 20x. In the same episode, the infrastructure papers: Fire-Flyer AI-HPC, the cluster DeepSeek co-designed, and 3FS, its distributed file system.

1:00 INTUITION — A screenshot of a page is a fixed-size object no matter how many words are on it. If a vision encoder can squeeze it into 100 tokens and a decoder can still read it, the image is a compressed form of the text. Old context could be stored as blurrier, smaller images, like human memory fading. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Compression ratio = text tokens of the ground truth / vision tokens fed to the decoder. Precision measured with edit distance: precision = 1 - EditDistance(pred, gt) / len(gt), roughly. DeepEncoder modes set vision tokens: verify the exact mode names and counts in the paper (Tiny 64, Small 100, Base 256, Large 400, and a tiled Gundam mode). Decoder: DeepSeek3B-MoE-A570M, about 570M active. Infra: Fire-Flyer 2 uses about 10,000 PCIe A100s with custom HFReduce all-reduce; verify the paper's cost and energy claims vs DGX-A100. 3FS: verify the aggregate read throughput figure in its README.

5:00 CODE — On RunPod 1x RTX 4090. Load deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-OCR with transformers trust_remote_code (follow the model card's inference snippet; it pins specific versions). Build a test set: 30 pages rendered from known text with PIL at fixed font, ranging from 300 to 3000 text tokens. For each page and each mode, run OCR, count text tokens of the ground truth with the model's tokenizer, compute compression ratio and edit-distance precision. Then infra: draw the Fire-Flyer 2 topology and the 3FS architecture from the papers, and run 3FS's fio-style benchmark only if a multi-node setup is available, otherwise read its published numbers.

8:30 RECEIPT — My precision vs compression ratio curve must match the paper's headline: around 97 percent below 10x and falling to around 60 percent near 20x. I overlay my 30 points on those two published anchors. Also check that Fox-style rendered pages give higher precision than messy real scans, and say so.

10:30 MEASURE — Scatter: precision vs compression ratio colored by mode. Second plot: tokens needed to represent a 10-page PDF as text vs as vision tokens per mode. Infra diagram with the three numbers that matter: GPUs, network, storage throughput.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Vision tokens can store text at around 10x compression with little loss, which suggests a path to cheaper long context, and DeepSeek's cluster and storage are co-designed with the model. Interview line: DeepSeek-OCR shows about 97 percent OCR precision under 10x text-to-vision compression, a proof of concept for optical context compression.
12:45 NEXT — Next: DeepSeek in miniature: putting it together

gotchas: The model's remote code pins transformers and flash-attn versions, a mismatched install fails in confusing ways, use the model card's environment; counting text tokens with a different tokenizer changes the ratio, use the model's own; rendered clean pages flatter the model compared to real scans.
interview_q: What is optical context compression? Rendering text as an image and encoding it into far fewer vision tokens than the text would need; DeepSeek-OCR shows the text can be decoded back at about 97% precision below 10x compression, suggesting older context could be stored as images to save tokens.
explainer: Here is a page with a thousand tokens of text. As text tokens, it costs a thousand slots in the context.
Render the same page as an image. The vision encoder turns it into just one hundred tokens.
The decoder reads those hundred tokens and writes the text back out. We compare it to the original letter by letter.
Below ten times compression it gets about ninety seven percent right. At twenty times, about sixty percent.
The idea for long context: keep recent text sharp, and store older context as smaller, blurrier images.
Behind all of this is DeepSeek's own cluster, ten thousand GPUs with a custom network for all-reduce.
And a file system built to feed them, so data loading never becomes the bottleneck.

hook: Some DeepSeek ideas pay off at 1 billion parameters. Others need hundreds of GPUs to matter. Here is my ablation table.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Some DeepSeek ideas pay off at 1 billion parameters. Others need hundreds of GPUs to matter. Here is my ablation table.

0:15 QUESTION — This module rebuilt DeepSeekMoE, MLA, MTP, FP8, DSA, mHC and Engram one at a time. Project P6 asks the real question: under a fixed compute budget at small scale, which of them still help? Labs care about this because ablations at small scale decide what goes into the big run.

1:00 INTUITION — A fair race. Every variant gets the same FLOPs, the same tokens, the same data order and the same tuning effort. Then we add one idea at a time, like a staircase, and measure each step with error bars. Ideas built for systems problems at scale, like DualPipe, should show nothing here, and that is a result too. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Fixed budget: C = 6 * N_active * D plus attention FLOPs, same C for every variant. Active-param matching for MoE vs dense. Effect size per step: delta = loss_variant - loss_prev, with paired seeds (same data order per seed) and SE from M14E04. Report delta in nats and as an effective compute multiplier: the factor k such that the dense baseline at k*C reaches the variant's loss, read off the dense scaling curve from M15E02.

4:30 CODE — On RunPod 4x GPU with FSDP from M10. configs/: dense.yaml (Llama-style, GQA), moe.yaml (DeepSeekMoE + MLA), moe_mtp.yaml, moe_mtp_dsa.yaml, moe_mtp_mhc.yaml, moe_mtp_engram.yaml. One train.py with flags. 3 seeds each at the ~0.5B-active scale on FineWeb-Edu. Log val loss, tokens/s, KV bytes per token, expert load imbalance, grad norm. Dense baseline also at 0.5x and 2x compute to build the compute-multiplier curve.

8:00 RECEIPT — Receipt one: the dense baseline's val loss lands where my M15E02 scaling fit predicts for this budget, within 0.02 nats. Receipt two: the MoE variant's load imbalance stays under 1.2 with aux-loss-free balancing. Receipt three: each row's CI is computed from 3 paired seeds, and any delta smaller than 2 SE is reported as 'no detectable effect'.

10:00 MEASURE — The table: variant, val loss mean and CI, compute multiplier, tokens/s, KV bytes per token, stability notes. Staircase plot of loss. Honest notes: DSA should matter only at long context, so I also report a 16k-context eval; mHC's gain in the paper was at 27B, and my result may be null.

11:45 TAKEAWAY — At small scale, MoE and MTP usually give measurable gains, while long-context and stability ideas show up only in the settings they target, and a clean null result is still a result. Interview line: I ablate under fixed compute with paired seeds and report effects as compute multipliers, so small-scale results are comparable to scaling laws.
12:30 NEXT — Next: How to read a paper in one hour
key_math: C = 6 N_active D (+ attention FLOPs) fixed; delta_i = L_i - L_{i-1} with paired-seed SE; compute multiplier k: L_dense(k C) = L_variant(C).
code_task: train.py --config {dense,moe,moe_mtp,moe_mtp_dsa,moe_mtp_mhc,moe_mtp_engram}.yaml --seed {0,1,2} with fixed token budget; ablation_table(runs) -> DataFrame(variant, loss_mean, ci_lo, ci_hi, multiplier, tok_s, kv_bytes); multiplier(loss, dense_curve) by interpolating log C.
receipt: Dense baseline val loss within 0.02 nats of the M15E02 scaling-fit prediction for the same C; MoE max/mean expert load < 1.2; every delta reported with a paired 95% CI, and deltas within 2 SE labeled as no detectable effect.
gotchas: Giving the new variant extra tuning (more lr sweeps) and not the baseline biases every ablation, use the same tuning budget; changing data order between variants adds noise that swamps small effects, fix the data seed per seed index; MoE wall-clock at small scale is often slower than dense even when it wins on FLOPs, report both.
interview_q: How do you decide whether an architecture change is worth putting in a big training run? Ablate it under fixed compute against a tuned baseline with multiple seeds, report the effect as a compute multiplier with confidence intervals, and check that the effect holds or grows across at least two scales.
explainer: Here is the race. Six variants, each with the same compute budget, the same tokens, and the same data order.
The baseline is a dense Llama style model. Its loss is our starting line.
Step one, swap in DeepSeek's mixture of experts and latent attention. The loss drops by a measurable step.
Step two, add multi-token prediction. Another smaller step, with error bars that just clear zero.
Then sparse attention, mHC and Engram, one at a time. Some steps are clear, some sit inside the noise.
We convert each step into a compute multiplier. How much more compute would the dense model need to match it?
The ideas built for huge clusters show little here. That tells us which tricks are about scale and which are about modeling.
